claim: The city spends money on bike lanes that should go to fixing roads.
finding: In the city's FY2025 adopted capital budget (the latest year in its open data), projects named for bikes or pedestrians total about $6.8 million, compared with about $98.1 million for road repair, and both are mostly paid for with borrowed (bond) money. Almost all of the bike total, $6.5 million, is one project to repave the University Avenue bikeway. The road repair total is also essentially one citywide project, "Resurfacing of City Streets". Separately, the FY2027 General Fund budget cut $2.6 million from the Transportation Department's multimodal team, which the IBA says eliminates new bikeway installations.
caveat: The city's capital budget data leaves out regional bikeways built by SANDAG, most grant-funded bike projects (such as the roughly $25 million Imperial Avenue Bikeway, paid for with TransNet sales tax and a state Active Transportation Program grant, and a $3.5 million SANDAG award for the Chollas Creek to Bayshore Bikeway), and street maintenance paid from the operating budget.

claim: Pensions are why the city is broke.
finding: The city's required pension payment for FY2027 is $563.2 million, up $30.0 million from FY2026; the proposed budget put the General Fund's share at 17.7% of General Fund spending, and the IBA names the higher payment as one of two reasons the FY2027 gap grew. But most of the payment is paying off the past, employees already pay about half of each year's new benefits, and reform has happened twice. Four things the documents show:
caveat: This shows how big the payment is and where the shortfall came from, not whether the benefits are too generous or what a 401(k)-style plan would cost instead; the shortfall is owed for benefits already earned, so moving new hires to a different plan would not remove it.

claim: City Hall is bloated with managers.
finding: The city's budget data does not give a clean count of managers over time, so this claim cannot be checked directly against city figures. The closest city number is the IBA's FY2027 snapshot: 833 of 12,628.5 standard-hour positions (6.6%) are unclassified and unrepresented, a group the IBA says is commonly used as shorthand for management. The IBA also found that these positions made up a larger share of the FY2027 job cuts (37.0% of the net reduction) than of the workforce. An Axios San Diego article of December 12, 2024 ran under the headline "Amid $200 million annual deficit, San Diego managers have grown 461% in 10 years"; the article itself was not accessible, so how it defines managers is unverified, and it is a news analysis, not a city figure.
caveat: Unclassified is a civil-service category rather than a job title (it includes, for example, all 135 City Council office positions), so it is only a rough stand-in for managers.

claim: The trash fee is a cash grab to pay for other city spending.
finding: The IBA says trash fee money pays only for trash collection, but because the General Fund used to pay for collection, the fee freed the General Fund from most of that cost; the FY2026 budget counted on moving $73.8 million of collection costs out of the General Fund. FY2026 was the first year in city history that some residents paid for trash collection directly, under service rules changed by Measure B in 2022. On June 8, 2026 the City Council approved a lawsuit settlement that lowers the fee from July 2027. The settlement brings back some General Fund subsidy, which the IBA puts at about $10.8 million in FY2028 after other savings.
caveat: The IBA says the General Fund's eventual cost could change with labor contracts, pension assumptions, fuel, fleet and disposal costs.

claim: Homelessness spending is swallowing the city budget.
finding: The city's data shows the homelessness department's General Fund budget at $49.1 million in FY2021, $18.1 million in FY2022 and $53.2 million in FY2026, about 2.5% of General Fund spending that year. The IBA says the FY2022 drop came from removing one-time federal COVID-19 relief, not from program cuts. The FY2027 adopted budget gives the department $62.0 million, after the May Revision swapped a $3.75 million placeholder cut for specific cuts. The IBA notes that much of the department's budget is repaid from hotel-tax (TOT) revenue, including Measure C funds.
caveat: This counts only the department's General Fund budget, so it leaves out state, federal and county grants and Housing Commission spending, and it shows money budgeted, not results.
